Economist here. The number of people who've tried to explain to me why well-established results in economics aren't true is so huge that I've long since stopped counting them. I'm a well-trained professional, but I realised a long time ago that in discussions on economic matters it's easier just to keep quiet. There's no point in discussing economics on Voat, for example, because almost everyone here is obsessed with some political viewpoint or other, and people here would rather argue than discuss carefully. The economic views of the extreme right wing (most Voaters) are as illiterate as those of the left (many Redditors), and there's really no point in saying anything, because if you say anything you just get dogpiled by a bunch of other semi-educated crotch-scratchers.

Now, in answer to your particular question, the most ridiculous thing that anyone outside my profession has claimed to know more about than me is the modelling of economic time series using various bits of fancy statistics. It's safe to say that I'm highly competent in this area, but I once had a student (actually a trainee at one of these "professional development conferences" that investment bankers seem to love - I was the token "academic economist" on the "panel") suggest that two obviously cointegrated time series could be well modeled by a simple linear regression. He got quite vocal about this and attempted to suggest that I was a fraud who didn't understand my subject when I tried to explain that this wasn't a good idea. It wasn't a pleasant experience.

well as a fellow economist, I can say that there aren't a whole lot of "well-established results", on the macro level at least. Economists in general are often blind to what aspects of their curriculum are scientific, and what is theoretical and only weakly supported by weak methods/data. There haven't been too many great economic experiments, as Earth is a shitty lab and policy makers aren't scientists.

But you are right on in that there will never be a productive discussion regarding economics on Voat or that other site due to the fact people generally dont try to understand their biases and that real science is the aim of the subject.

Generally agree. I think you're probably right when you say that "there aren't a whole lot of 'well-established results'". Everything we do is annoyingly complicated and we're forever having to deal with all sorts of background noise. I think what I was really thinking is that there are a lot of results that we can be fairly sure are generally sound, and so we're better to start from a presumption of their truth and then try to work out what's going on in individual cases that seem to be exceptions. For example, I think that the reasoning supporting comparative advantage is pretty strong, and I'd probably class comparative advantage as a "well-established result", so I think we're probably wiser to approach questions around trade by starting with the view that "comparative advantage suggests..." and then asking "so what's going on here that makes this situation different?", rather than starting from the position that "Ricardo's obviously wrong"!

I agree that it would be nice if we could do more experiments, but I also feel that part of the fun of economics is that we often have to proceed entirely by observation. As Yogi Berra remarked, "You can observe a lot by just watching".
